classic-mixed-vegetables-canned-reduced-.title: Classic Mixed Vegetables, Canned, Reduced Sodium, Cooked, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: The “Classic mixed vegetables” canned product is a blend of carrots, corn, peas and green beans that is cooked without added fat and with reduced sodium. The vegetables are blanched, quickly sealed in airtight cans, and heat‑processed to retain flavor, color, and nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix typically includes carrot, corn, green pea and green bean, providing a broad spectrum of vitamins and minerals.
Reduced sodium is achieved by using a modest amount of salt and natural flavor enhancers.
Fat‑free processing makes the product low‑calorie and suitable for weight‑management diets.
Rapid thermal processing preserves most B‑vitamins and carotenoids.
Cans are made of aluminum alloy with an internal coating that prevents oxidation and flavor loss.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A and C
items.content: Carrots and corn supply beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, while peas provide vitamin C, supporting immune function and vision.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: The vegetable blend offers both soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt helps maintain healthy blood pressure and reduces kidney strain.

items.title: No added fat
items.content: Absence of added fat makes the product suitable for low‑fat and calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains potassium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals support heart function, muscle activity, and fluid balance.

items.title: Allergy to individual vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may react to carrot, corn, or pea components.

items.title: Preservative content
items.content: While no artificial preservatives are added, a small amount of citric acid may be used in some markets to stabilize pH.

items.title: Bacterial safety after opening
items.content: Once opened, the product should be refrigerated and consumed within 3‑4 days to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The vegetables can be eaten straight from the can, added to soups, stews, salads, or used as a side dish for meat. They also reheat well in the microwave or on the stovetop with a splash of water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the contents in a sealed container in the refrigerator and use within a few days.

cranberry-juice-blend-100-juice-with-cal.title: Cranberry Juice Blend, 100% Juice, with Calcium Added

content.title: About
content.content: Cranberry Juice Blend is a 100% juice made from selected cranberries, fortified with calcium to support bone health. The juice contains no added sugar, preservatives, or artificial flavors. Its bright red color and characteristic sweet‑tart taste make it a great daily beverage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cranberries are rich in proanthocyanidins, which help maintain urinary tract health.
Cranberry juice has been traditionally used in North America as a preventive measure against urinary infections.
Calcium fortification increases the nutritional value without altering the flavor.
Cranberries are a good source of vitamin C, which boosts immunity.
The juice is packaged in dark bottles to protect light‑sensitive antioxidants.

items.title: Urinary tract support
items.content: Cranberry phytochemicals prevent bacteria from adhering to the bladder walls.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C enhances immune defense and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Added calcium contributes to stronger bones and teeth, especially important for those with higher mineral needs.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Cranberry polyphenols help neutralize free radicals, slowing oxidative processes in the body.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: The juice contains no added sugar, making it suitable for moderate consumption by people monitoring glucose levels.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature of cranberry juice may irritate the stomach in individuals with high sensitivity.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Cranberries can increase the effect of anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin); consult a doctor if you are on such medication.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cranberries.

items.title: Excess calcium
items.content: Too much calcium may contribute to kidney stone formation in predisposed persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the juice chilled as a refreshing drink, add it to smoothies, cocktails, or use it as a base for non‑alcoholic mixed drinks. It can be diluted with water to reduce acidity.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 1 °C to 4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days. Keep away from direct sunlight.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg, deviled (1954) is a classic dish consisting of hard‑boiled eggs, halved and filled with a mixture of yolk, mayonnaise, mustard, and spices. The name references the year when the recipe gained popularity in the United States.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first deviled egg recipes appeared in 19th‑century cookbooks, but the 1954 version spread widely through magazine publications.
Traditional fillings include vinegar, paprika, and finely chopped onion.
Deviled eggs are a staple on holiday tables, especially Easter and Thanksgiving.
Various countries have their own twists: Japan adds soy sauce, Mexico uses chili and lime.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The yolk contains B12, B6, and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Source of choline
items.content: Choline is important for brain health and liver function.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: The yolk supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can benefit cardiovascular health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk help protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor Salmonella; ensure eggs are fully cooked.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol, so individuals with high cholesterol should moderate intake.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Mayonnaise‑based fillings can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve deviled eggs chilled as an appetizer. Garnish with paprika, fresh herbs, or olive slices. They pair well with crackers, salads, and light soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared deviled eggs in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Discard if they develop an off odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Manicotti are large pasta tubes that are usually stuffed with various fillings. This version is filled with creamy cheese and served without sauce, allowing the delicate cheese flavor and pasta texture to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Italian “manicotto,” meaning “sleeve.”
Traditional fillings include ricotta, spinach or meat, but cheese‑only fillings are becoming increasingly popular.
The tubes are made from durum wheat semolina, giving them a firm bite.
Without sauce, manicotti are often served cold as a salad or as a standalone appetizer.
In Italy there is a baked version called “manicotti al forno,” but our product is intentionally sauce‑free.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The cheese filling provides both dairy and plant protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Cream cheese is rich in calcium, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Semolina pasta supplies B1, B2 and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The product contains no added sugars, making it suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Durum wheat contributes a modest amount of fiber that helps digestion.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream cheese contains lactose, so individuals with intolerance should choose alternatives.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional pasta is made from wheat and contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The cheese filling adds calories; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cream cheese is often salted, so those monitoring sodium intake should be aware.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Manicotti can be enjoyed warm or cold. They work well as a standalone dish, tossed into salads, or used as a filling for sandwiches. For a softer texture, gently heat in the microwave or steam briefly to melt the cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep manicotti in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 3 days. Frozen portions retain quality for up to 2 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potatoes are a dish made from boiled potatoes that are mashed to a smooth consistency, often enriched with butter, milk or cream, and sometimes seasoned with salt and pepper. It is commonly served as a side dish to meat, fish, or vegetable entrees.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are the fourth most produced crop worldwide after rice, wheat, and corn.
Mashed potatoes have been prepared independently in many cultures; Europe has records of mashed potatoes dating back to the Middle Ages.
Butter makes the mash richer and creamier, but it can be substituted with plant‑based oils for a lighter version.
Mashed potatoes are a staple in infant and toddler diets because of their soft texture and easy digestibility.
In some countries, such as the United States, mashed potatoes are often topped with cheese, garlic, or herbs for extra flavor.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide a good amount of potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Potatoes contain vitamin C, an antioxidant that helps boost the immune system.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Mashed potatoes supply slow‑releasing energy thanks to their complex carbohydrate content.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The skin and a small portion of the flesh contain dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Potatoes provide vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Mashed potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When salt is added, the dish can become a source of excess sodium, which may affect blood pressure.

items.title: Dairy allergy or intolerance
items.content: If milk, cream, or butter are used, individuals with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort.

items.title: Nutrient loss
items.content: Over‑mixing can cause oxidation and loss of some vitamins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve mashed potatoes hot as a side to meat, fish, or vegetables. Enhance flavor with butter, milk, cream, cheese, garlic, or fresh herbs. For a lighter version, use plant‑based milk or broth.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store mashed potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat gently, adding a splash of milk or broth to restore creaminess. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato salad made with any type of fat‑free dressing is a dish of boiled potatoes mixed with vegetables and a light, no‑fat dressing. It is popular as a side dish or a light meal, especially for those watching their fat intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato salad is often served cold, but it can also be enjoyed slightly warm.
Fat‑free dressings may include yogurt, kefir, mustard, vinegar or lemon juice, making the dish more diet‑friendly.
The classic Russian “Olivier” salad is a variation of potato salad that traditionally uses mayonnaise.
Potatoes retain most of their vitamins when boiled with the skin on and not overcooked.
The salad can be varied with herbs, eggs, carrots, celery or beans.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Potatoes provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using a fat‑free dressing makes the salad suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Potatoes and added vegetables supply fiber that benefits digestion.

items.title: Energy‑providing carbs
items.content: The carbohydrates in potatoes provide a quick source of energy, useful before physical activity.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to potatoes, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Excessive salt in the dressing can raise blood pressure; keep salt levels moderate.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad as a standalone dish, as a side to meat or fish, or in sandwiches. It stores well chilled and can be garnished with fresh herbs, olives or low‑fat cottage cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Over time the flavor and texture may change, so it is best prepared in portions.

content.title: About
content.content: Turmeric (Curcuma longa) is the rhizome of a tropical plant in the ginger family, native to South Asia. The rhizome is dried and ground into a bright yellow or orange powder with a warm, earthy, slightly bitter flavor. Turmeric is added to curries, rice, soups, vegetable dishes, and drinks, and fresh root is grated like ginger.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turmeric is related to ginger.
Turmeric gives dishes a bright golden-yellow color and is part of curry.
Curcumin, the main coloring compound, makes up only a few percent of the rhizome by weight.
Black pepper contains piperine, which increases the absorption of curcumin.
Turmeric leaves stains on fabric, plastic, and skin that are hard to remove.

items.title: Contains curcumin
items.content: Curcumin is a compound with antioxidant properties that is actively studied.

items.title: Studied for anti-inflammatory properties
items.content: Curcumin is studied for anti-inflammatory effects, but evidence is still limited.

items.title: Traditionally supports digestion
items.content: In traditional cooking and folk practice, turmeric is used to support digestion.

items.title: Adds flavor and color
items.content: A pinch of turmeric colors dishes and adds aroma with almost no calories.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: In small amounts, turmeric provides iron and manganese.

items.title: Supplements and the liver
items.content: Concentrated curcumin supplements, especially with piperine, have in rare cases been linked to liver damage; discuss them with a doctor.

items.title: Stones
items.content: Turmeric may increase gallbladder contraction and contains oxalates, so people with gallstones or kidney stones should consult a doctor.

items.title: Medications
items.content: Turmeric may affect how anticoagulants, diabetes medications, and others work; consult a doctor if you take medications.

items.title: Spice quality
items.content: In some cases turmeric is adulterated with harmful dyes, so buy it from trusted producers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add turmeric to curries, rice, soups, vegetables, eggs, sauces, and golden milk. For better absorption, combine it with fat and a pinch of black pepper. Fresh root can be grated or sliced. Keep in mind that turmeric stains hands and dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ground turmeric in an airtight jar in a dry, dark, cool place. Keep fresh root in the refrigerator for two to three weeks or freeze it. Discard powder that has lost its color and smell.
